faq.q: Can I use this to check my child's vision?
faq.a: This test requires subjective responses and letter recognition, so it's suitable for children who can reliably identify letters (typically age 5-6 and older). For younger children, objective screening methods like retinoscopy performed by a pediatric optometrist are more appropriate.

faq.q: Why do I see differently on my phone vs computer?
faq.a: Different displays have different color temperatures, gamma curves, and pixel densities. OLED screens typically show more vibrant colors than LCD. For consistent results, use the same device and ensure brightness is set to a comfortable, typical viewing level.

faq.q: Is my input data private when using this tool?
faq.a: Yes. Processing runs entirely in your local browser memory. Your inputs and configuration parameters are never uploaded to our servers.

faq.q: Does this tool work on mobile devices and tablets?
faq.a: Yes. The interface is responsive and works across all modern mobile, tablet, and desktop web browsers.

articleHtml:
The Physics of Color: Why Red and Green Reveal Your Prescription

Chromatic aberration isn't just an optical defect — it's a diagnostic tool. Your eye's lens focuses different wavelengths of light at slightly different points. By exploiting this physics, we can detect whether your eye is over-focused (myopic) or under-focused (hyperopic).

The Green Light Principle

Green light (550nm) has a shorter wavelength than red light (700nm). Due to chromatic aberration, your eye focuses green light slightly behind red light. If green appears clearer, your eye may be slightly over-focused (tending toward myopia/nearsightedness).

Chapter 1: Understanding Chromatic Aberration

When white light passes through a convex lens (like your eye's crystalline lens), each wavelength bends at a different angle. Violet light bends most, focusing closest to the lens. Red light bends least, focusing farthest away. This creates a spectrum of focal points — the Longitudinal Chromatic Aberration.

Your eye's total power spans approximately 2.5 diopters from red to violet focus. This means a "perfect" focus for red light would leave green light 2.5 diopters over-focused.

Chapter 2: Interpreting Your Results

  • Green Clearer: Your eye's focus point is behind the retina for green light. This suggests slight myopia (nearsightedness) or over-correction. Consider reducing minus prescription.
  • Red Clearer: Your eye's focus point is in front of the retina for red light. This suggests slight hyperopia (farsightedness) or under-correction. Consider increasing plus prescription.
  • Equal Clarity: Your eye is properly focused for the test distance. The letters appear equally sharp because both wavelengths fall equidistant from the retina.

Clinical Precision

Professional refraction uses this principle at a finer level. The optometrist asks you "better with green or red?" while adjusting lenses in 0.25D steps until you answer "equal." That lens power represents your optimal correction.

Chapter 3: Why This Test Uses Split Screen

Traditional duochrome tests show the entire letter on either all-red or all-green backgrounds. Our split-screen version allows you to compare clarity side-by-side in real-time, making it easier to detect subtle differences.

Chapter 4: Limitations

This screening tool cannot replace professional refraction because:

  • It doesn't account for astigmatism (which requires cylinder correction)
  • Monitor color calibration varies between devices
  • Ambient lighting affects perceived contrast
  • It can't measure absolute refraction value, only relative balance
